title: Number systems
subject: Mathematics
summary: Real numbers include rational and irrational numbers, and they can be located on a number line.
points: Rational numbers can be written as p/q with q ≠ 0; irrational numbers cannot.
Every real number has a decimal expansion that terminates or repeats (rational) or neither (irrational).
Between any two real numbers there are infinitely many rational and irrational numbers.
Rationalisation removes surds from a denominator by multiplying by the conjugate.
Laws of exponents extend to rational exponents.
example: √2 is irrational: its decimal expansion neither terminates nor repeats.
mistakes: Calling every square root irrational; √9 = 3 is rational.
Assuming a terminating decimal cannot be rational.

title: Coordinate geometry: the Cartesian plane
subject: Mathematics
summary: Points in a plane are located by an ordered pair of coordinates measured from two perpendicular axes.
points: The x-axis is horizontal and the y-axis vertical; they meet at the origin (0, 0).
Coordinates are written (abscissa, ordinate) and signs decide the quadrant.
A point on the x-axis has y = 0; a point on the y-axis has x = 0.
Cartesian geometry links algebra and geometry so figures can be studied with coordinates.
example: (−3, 4) lies in the second quadrant because x is negative and y positive.
mistakes: Reversing the order of x and y.
Forgetting that the origin belongs to no quadrant.

title: Heron's formula
subject: Mathematics
summary: Heron's formula gives the area of a triangle from the lengths of its three sides.
points: First find the semi-perimeter s = (a + b + c)/2.
Area = √[s(s − a)(s − b)(s − c)].
The formula works for any triangle and is useful when height is unknown.
For a quadrilateral, split it into two triangles and add the areas.
example: Sides 3, 4, 5 give s = 6 and area = √(6 × 3 × 2 × 1) = 6 square units.
mistakes: Using the perimeter instead of the semi-perimeter.
Forgetting to take the square root.

title: Areas of parallelograms and triangles
subject: Mathematics
summary: Parallelograms on the same base and between the same parallels have equal area, and a triangle is half the parallelogram on the same base.
points: Area of a parallelogram is base × height.
Area of a triangle is ½ × base × height.
Figures on the same base and between the same parallels have equal areas.
A median divides a triangle into two triangles of equal area.
example: A triangle and a parallelogram on the same base and between the same parallels: the triangle has half the area.
mistakes: Using a slant side as the height.
Assuming equal perimeters mean equal areas.

title: Geometrical constructions
subject: Mathematics
summary: Constructions use compass and straightedge to build angles, triangles and circles with given conditions.
points: Bisecting an angle and drawing a perpendicular bisector are the basic constructions.
A triangle can be constructed from SSS, SAS, ASA or RHS data.
Some constructions also require a given perimeter or a given base angle sum.
Justification requires stating which construction steps guarantee the result.
A ruler and compass only; measurement is used to check, not to draw.
example: Construct a triangle with sides 4 cm, 5 cm and 6 cm by drawing the base and arcs from its ends.
mistakes: Erasing construction arcs, which are part of the answer.
Skipping the justification step.

title: Circles: chords and angles
subject: Mathematics
summary: Equal chords subtend equal angles at the centre, and the perpendicular from the centre bisects a chord.
points: Equal chords of a circle are equidistant from the centre.
The angle subtended by an arc at the centre is double the angle at any point on the remaining circle.
Angles in the same segment are equal.
The angle in a semicircle is a right angle.
A cyclic quadrilateral has opposite angles summing to 180°.
example: If a chord subtends 80° at the centre, it subtends 40° at a point on the major arc.
mistakes: Doubling instead of halving the central angle.
Assuming every quadrilateral is cyclic.

title: Statistics: presentation of data
subject: Mathematics
summary: Data can be presented as frequency tables, bar graphs, histograms and frequency polygons.
points: Ungrouped data lists values; grouped data uses class intervals.
Class mark is the midpoint of a class interval.
A histogram shows continuous grouped data with adjacent bars.
A frequency polygon joins midpoints of the tops of the bars.
Mean, median and mode are the three measures of central tendency.
example: For classes 10–20, 20–30 the class marks are 15 and 25.
mistakes: Leaving gaps between bars in a histogram.
Using the class limit instead of the class mark.

title: Surface areas and volumes
subject: Mathematics
summary: Solids such as cubes, cuboids, cylinders, cones and spheres have standard surface area and volume formulas.
points: Curved surface area covers only the curved part; total surface area includes flat faces.
Volume is measured in cubic units and capacity in litres.
A hollow object's volume is the difference between outer and inner volumes.
Composite solids are handled by adding or subtracting the parts.
example: A cylinder of radius 7 cm and height 10 cm has volume 22/7 × 49 × 10 = 1540 cm³.
mistakes: Using diameter instead of radius.
Confusing CSA with TSA for a cylinder.

title: Structure of the atom
subject: Science
summary: Atoms contain protons, neutrons and electrons, and their arrangement explains valency and isotopes.
points: Protons and neutrons form the nucleus; electrons occupy shells around it.
Atomic number is the number of protons; mass number is protons plus neutrons.
Electrons fill shells in the 2, 8, 8 pattern for the first twenty elements.
Valency depends on the number of electrons needed to complete the outermost shell.
Isotopes have the same atomic number but different mass numbers.

formulas.name: Valency
formulas.expr: electrons to gain, lose or share to complete the octet

example: Sodium (Z = 11) has configuration 2, 8, 1 and loses one electron to form Na⁺.
mistakes: Confusing atomic number with mass number.
Thinking isotopes differ chemically in every way.

title: Diversity in living organisms
subject: Science
summary: Living organisms are classified into five kingdoms and further into phyla, classes and species by shared features.
points: Classification uses cell type, body organisation, mode of nutrition and reproduction.
The five kingdoms are Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia.
Plants are divided into thallophytes, bryophytes, pteridophytes, gymnosperms and angiosperms.
Animals are divided into invertebrates and vertebrates by the presence of a backbone.
Nomenclature follows binomial names in Latin.
example: Frogs are amphibians: they live in water and on land and breathe through skin and lungs.
mistakes: Classifying fungi as plants.
Using common names instead of binomial names.

title: Why do we fall ill?
subject: Science
summary: Health is a state of physical and mental well-being, and disease results from pathogens, deficiencies or environmental factors.
points: Infectious diseases spread through air, water, food, vectors and contact.
Non-infectious diseases include deficiency diseases and genetic disorders.
Immunisation trains the body's immune system against specific pathogens.
Prevention through sanitation, clean water and vaccination is more effective than cure alone.
Antibiotics work against bacteria, not viruses.
example: Malaria spreads through the bite of an infected female Anopheles mosquito.
mistakes: Taking antibiotics for a viral cold.
Assuming all diseases are infectious.

title: Natural resources
subject: Science
summary: Air, water, soil, forests and minerals are natural resources that must be used sustainably.
points: Resources are renewable (sunlight, wind, biomass) or non-renewable (fossil fuels, minerals).
The water cycle and groundwater recharge sustain freshwater supply.
Soil erosion and pollution reduce fertility and can be controlled by contour ploughing and afforestation.
The greenhouse effect and ozone depletion are consequences of air pollution.
Sustainable use means meeting present needs without destroying future supply.
example: Planting trees on a slope reduces soil erosion by slowing runoff.
mistakes: Calling groundwater unlimited.
Confusing global warming with ozone hole formation.

title: Improvement in food resources
subject: Science
summary: Food production can be raised through better crop varieties, nutrients, irrigation, pest control and animal husbandry.
points: Crop variety improvement uses hybridisation and selection for higher yield and disease resistance.
Macro and micro nutrients replenish soil fertility; organic manure improves soil texture.
Irrigation methods include canal, tube well, drip and sprinkler.
Integrated pest management reduces chemical pesticide use.
Animal husbandry covers cattle, poultry and fish farming.
example: Drip irrigation saves water by delivering it directly to plant roots.
mistakes: Thinking fertiliser alone guarantees higher yield.
Ignoring crop rotation for soil health.

title: Sources of energy
subject: Science
summary: Energy sources are renewable or non-renewable, and good sources are cheap, safe and environmentally clean.
points: Fossil fuels are non-renewable and release carbon dioxide and pollutants.
Solar, wind, hydro, biomass and geothermal are renewable sources.
A solar cooker and solar cell both use sunlight but for different purposes.
Wind energy needs a minimum wind speed and large areas.
Biogas from anaerobic digestion provides clean fuel in rural areas.
example: A solar cell converts light directly into electricity, while a solar water heater uses heat.
mistakes: Calling all renewable sources pollution free at every stage.
Confusing a solar cell with a solar heater.

title: Management of natural resources
subject: Science
summary: Sustainable management of forests, water, coal and petroleum protects resources for future generations.
points: The three Rs — reduce, reuse, recycle — reduce waste.
Chipko and other movements show community participation in forest protection.
Water harvesting collects rainwater for groundwater recharge.
Dams generate power and irrigation but displace people and silt up.
Biodiversity must be preserved because species are interdependent.
example: Rooftop rainwater harvesting recharges groundwater and reduces urban flooding.
mistakes: Assuming dams have no environmental cost.
Thinking recycling alone solves resource depletion.

title: Forest society and colonialism
subject: History
summary: Colonial forest laws restricted villagers' use of forests for timber and revenue, provoking resistance.
points: The Indian Forest Act 1865 and 1878 gave the state control over forests.
Villagers lost rights to graze, collect fuel and practise shifting cultivation.
Scientific forestry replaced mixed forests with single-species plantations.
The Bastar rebellion of 1910 opposed forest reservation.
Forest villages were used for labour, worsening their condition.
example: The Bastar rebellion saw villagers attack forest offices and resist reservation of forests.
mistakes: Thinking forest laws protected villagers' rights.
Ignoring the role of grazing and fuel collection.

title: Pastoralists in the modern world
subject: History
summary: Pastoral communities move with their herds and were affected by colonial borders, grazing restrictions and settlement policies.
points: Pastoralists move seasonally between pastures to avoid overgrazing.
Colonial governments saw mobility as disorder and restricted grazing land.
Borders cut across traditional migration routes.
Pastoralists adapted by settling, changing herds or taking up trade and labour.
Their knowledge of dryland ecology is valuable for sustainable land use.
example: Gujjar herders moving between summer and winter pastures were affected by new forest boundaries.
mistakes: Calling pastoralists wanderers without pattern.
Ignoring their adaptation to modern conditions.

title: Print culture and the modern world
subject: History
summary: Printing made texts cheap and abundant, spreading ideas, literacy and new forms of public debate.
points: Woodblock printing existed in China before movable type in Europe.
Gutenberg's press made books cheaper and faster to produce.
Print spread religious reform, scientific ideas and political criticism.
In India, print helped vernacular literature and nationalist opinion.
Censorship showed that print was seen as politically powerful.
example: Newspapers and pamphlets carried nationalist arguments to a wide Indian readership.
mistakes: Crediting Gutenberg with inventing printing entirely.
Ignoring vernacular print in India.

title: The age of industrialisation
subject: History
summary: Industrialisation changed production, work and cities, and in India it took a colonial form.
points: Proto-industrialisation was production by merchants for export before factories.
Factories concentrated machines, workers and discipline in one place.
In India, textile mills grew in Bombay and Calcutta in the nineteenth century.
Handicraft workers faced declining demand and shifted to other work.
Industrialisation created new social classes and urban problems.
example: Indian hand weavers lost markets as machine-made British cloth entered India.
mistakes: Assuming factories replaced handicrafts overnight.
Ignoring colonial trade policy.

title: Climate of India
subject: Geography
summary: India has a tropical monsoon climate with seasonal reversal of winds and large regional variation.
points: The monsoon arrives from the south-west in June and withdraws from the north by October.
The Western Ghats and Himalayas influence rainfall distribution.
Seasons are winter, summer, south-west monsoon and retreating monsoon.
Mawsynram and Cherrapunji receive very high rainfall due to relief.
El Niño and the Indian Ocean Dipole affect monsoon strength.
example: The windward Western Ghats get heavy rain while the Deccan plateau lies in its rain shadow.
mistakes: Saying all of India gets rain at the same time.
Confusing climate with weather.

title: Drainage
subject: Geography
summary: India's rivers are grouped as Himalayan and peninsular river systems, shaping plains, deltas and agriculture.
points: Himalayan rivers are perennial because they are fed by snow and rain.
Peninsular rivers are seasonal and largely rain-fed.
The Ganga, Indus and Brahmaputra systems drain the northern plains.
The Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri and Narmada drain the peninsula.
Deltas form where rivers deposit sediment at the sea.
example: The Ganga–Brahmaputra delta is the largest delta in the world.
mistakes: Calling all Indian rivers perennial.
Confusing tributaries with distributaries.

title: Population of India
subject: Geography
summary: India's population is large and unevenly distributed, with a young age structure and growing urban share.
points: Density is highest in the northern plains and coastal lowlands.
Birth rate, death rate and migration change population size.
Sex ratio and literacy are key population characteristics.
A large young population is a demographic dividend if educated and employed.
Population policy aims at health, education and family welfare.
example: Kerala has high density and high literacy, showing density does not imply poverty.
mistakes: Assuming high density always means low development.
Confusing growth rate with birth rate.

title: Resources and development
subject: Geography
summary: Resources are classified by origin, exhaustibility, ownership and development status, and must be used sustainably.
points: Resources may be renewable or non-renewable, individual or community owned, potential or developed.
Land degradation is caused by deforestation, overgrazing and mining.
Soil types include alluvial, black, red, laterite, arid and forest soils.
Soil erosion is controlled by contour ploughing, terracing and shelter belts.
Resource planning needs inventory, appropriate technology and matching with needs.
example: Black soil retains moisture and suits cotton, which is why it is called cotton soil.
mistakes: Classifying all resources as renewable.
Ignoring ownership as a basis of classification.

title: Water resources
subject: Geography
summary: Freshwater is scarce and unevenly distributed, so storage, irrigation and rainwater harvesting are essential.
points: Dams provide irrigation, power and flood control but displace people and cause silting.
Multipurpose river valley projects have both benefits and costs.
Rainwater harvesting recharges groundwater and reduces runoff.
Over-irrigation causes waterlogging and salinity.
Water scarcity results from overuse, pollution and unequal access.
example: Rooftop harvesting in Rajasthan's arid areas stores rainwater for the dry season.
mistakes: Thinking dams have only benefits.
Ignoring groundwater depletion.

title: Lifelines of national economy
subject: Geography
summary: Transport, communication and international trade link production and consumption across India and the world.
points: Roads are classified as national highways, state highways, district and village roads.
Railways carry bulk goods over long distances and are the main freight carrier.
Ports handle overseas trade; Kandla and Mumbai are major western ports.
Airways are fastest but costliest; pipelines carry oil and gas.
Tourism earns foreign exchange and supports local employment.
example: The Golden Quadrilateral connects Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai and Kolkata by highway.
mistakes: Confusing national and state highways.
Ignoring pipelines as a transport mode.

title: Working of institutions
subject: Civics
summary: In a democracy, the legislature, executive and judiciary each have defined powers and check one another.
points: Parliament makes laws and controls the executive.
The Prime Minister and Council of Ministers form the political executive.
The President is the head of state and acts on the advice of the Council of Ministers.
The judiciary interprets laws and protects fundamental rights.
Rules and procedures prevent any one institution from becoming all-powerful.
example: The Supreme Court can strike down a law that violates fundamental rights.
mistakes: Thinking the President makes policy personally.
Ignoring the judiciary's power of review.

title: Democratic rights
subject: Civics
summary: Fundamental rights protect citizens against arbitrary state power and are enforceable in court.
points: Rights include equality, freedom, against exploitation, religion, cultural and educational rights, and constitutional remedies.
The right to constitutional remedies lets citizens approach courts for enforcement.
Rights are not absolute; reasonable restrictions apply.
National Human Rights Commission and courts provide protection.
Rights apply to citizens and, in some cases, to all persons.
example: Article 32 allows a citizen to move the Supreme Court directly for enforcement of fundamental rights.
mistakes: Believing fundamental rights are unlimited.
Forgetting that some rights apply to non-citizens too.

title: Popular struggles and movements
subject: Civics
summary: Democracy is strengthened when people organise movements and pressure groups outside formal institutions.
points: The Nepal struggle of 2006 restored democracy through mass protest.
Bolivia's water war opposed privatisation of water supply.
Movements use protest, media, petitions and litigation.
Pressure groups pursue specific interests and influence policy.
Movements can complement parties but do not replace elections.
example: Bolivia's 2000 protests reversed a water privatisation contract.
mistakes: Thinking movements alone can govern.
Assuming all pressure groups are democratic in method.

title: The story of Village Palampur
subject: Economics
summary: Palampur illustrates production, farming, non-farm activities and the role of capital and labour in a village economy.
points: Production needs land, labour, capital and human capital.
Multiple cropping and modern inputs raise farm output.
Small farmers often borrow from moneylenders at high interest.
Non-farm activities include dairy, small manufacturing and transport.
Better infrastructure and credit support rural development.
example: A farmer using HYV seeds, fertiliser and tubewell irrigation produces more than one crop a year.
mistakes: Treating capital as only money.
Ignoring the role of irrigation in multiple cropping.

title: People as resource
subject: Economics
summary: People are a resource when their skills and health are developed, contributing to production and growth.
points: Human capital formation comes from education, health and training.
Educated and healthy workers are more productive.
Unemployment may be seasonal, disguised or educated unemployment.
Disguised unemployment means more workers than needed on a task.
Investment in education raises future income and national output.
example: Five workers doing a job that needs three is disguised unemployment.
mistakes: Calling all unemployment voluntary.
Confusing seasonal with disguised unemployment.

title: Poverty as a challenge
subject: Economics
summary: Poverty is measured by a minimum consumption level, and it has social as well as economic dimensions.
points: The poverty line is based on minimum calorie and consumption requirements.
Poverty is higher in rural areas and among certain social groups.
Causes include low growth, inequality, unemployment and lack of education.
Anti-poverty measures include employment schemes, food security and education.
Poverty is multidimensional: health, shelter, sanitation and dignity matter.
example: MGNREGA provides guaranteed wage employment to reduce rural poverty.
mistakes: Measuring poverty only by income.
Assuming poverty is uniform across regions.

title: Food security in India
subject: Economics
summary: Food security means availability, accessibility and affordability of food, supported by buffer stocks and the public distribution system.
points: The FCI procures grain at minimum support prices and stores buffer stocks.
The PDS distributes subsidised grain through fair price shops.
Antyodaya cards target the poorest households.
Buffer stocks stabilise prices and cover shortages.
Problems include leakages, exclusion errors and storage losses.
example: A drought year is cushioned by releasing buffer stock through fair price shops.
mistakes: Equating food security with food availability alone.
Ignoring leakages in the PDS.

title: Office tools: word processor, spreadsheet and presentation
subject: Computer Science
summary: Office software creates documents, calculates with data and presents information visually.
points: A word processor handles text formatting, tables, headers and mail merge.
A spreadsheet stores data in cells and recalculates formulas automatically.
Common spreadsheet functions include SUM, AVERAGE, MAX, MIN and IF.
A presentation tool builds slides with text, images, charts and transitions.
Saving in different formats and printing settings matter for sharing work.
example: =AVERAGE(B2:B6) gives the mean of marks in five cells.
mistakes: Typing values instead of formulas so totals do not update.
Forgetting that formulas begin with =.

title: Visual programming with Scratch
subject: Computer Science
summary: Scratch builds programs by snapping together blocks, teaching sequencing, loops, conditions and events.
points: Sprites are objects with costumes and scripts.
Blocks are grouped as motion, looks, sound, events, control, sensing, operators and variables.
Events such as 'when green flag clicked' start scripts.
Loops and conditions create repetition and decisions.
Variables and messages allow interaction between sprites.
example: A 'repeat 10 — move 10 steps' script makes a sprite walk across the stage.
mistakes: Placing blocks outside any event so nothing runs.
Forgetting to initialise variables before a loop.

title: English grammar: clauses, determiners and modals
subject: English
summary: Clauses combine subject and verb, determiners specify nouns, and modals express possibility, obligation and permission.
points: A main clause stands alone; a subordinate clause depends on it.
Noun, adjective and adverb clauses do different jobs in a sentence.
Determiners include articles, possessives, demonstratives and quantifiers.
Modals such as can, may, must, should and might show attitude rather than tense.
Subject–verb agreement and correct connectors are commonly tested.
example: "Although it rained, we played" has a subordinate clause followed by a main clause.
mistakes: Writing a sentence fragment as a main clause.
Using 'must' for past obligation instead of 'had to'.

title: English writing: analytical paragraph and story
subject: English
summary: Class 9–10 writing tasks include analytical paragraphs based on data, stories and descriptive pieces.
points: An analytical paragraph interprets a chart, table or graph in about 100–120 words.
It needs an opening statement, key comparisons and a conclusion.
A story needs a setting, characters, a complication and a resolution.
Descriptive writing uses sensory detail and varied sentence length.
Accuracy in tense and spelling matters more than long words.
example: An analytical paragraph on a bar graph notes the highest and lowest values and the overall trend.
mistakes: Describing every data point instead of the trend.
Writing a story without a complication.

title: Climate change
subject: Science
summary: Human emissions of greenhouse gases are warming the planet and changing rainfall, ice cover and sea level.
points: Carbon dioxide from fossil fuels and methane from agriculture are the main added greenhouse gases.
Warming raises sea level through thermal expansion and melting ice.
Impacts include heatwaves, erratic monsoons, droughts, floods and shifting crop zones.
Mitigation reduces emissions; adaptation prepares for unavoidable change.
International agreements set targets but depend on national action.
example: A glacier retreating over decades reduces dry-season river flow for downstream farmers.
mistakes: Confusing climate change with the ozone hole.
Assuming adaptation can replace mitigation.

title: Waste management
subject: Science
summary: Waste is managed by reducing, segregating, composting, recycling and safe disposal.
points: Biodegradable waste can be composted; non-biodegradable waste needs recycling or safe disposal.
Segregation at source makes recycling possible.
Landfills must be lined to prevent leachate reaching groundwater.
Plastic waste harms animals and blocks drains, worsening flooding.
The 3Rs and extended producer responsibility reduce waste generation.
example: Kitchen waste composted in a pit becomes manure instead of rotting in a landfill.
mistakes: Burning plastic, which releases toxic gases.
Mixing wet and dry waste so neither can be processed.

title: Disaster management
subject: Science
summary: Disaster management reduces risk before, during and after events such as floods, earthquakes, cyclones and fires.
points: Disasters may be natural or human-made and their impact depends on vulnerability.
Preparedness includes early warning, drills, evacuation plans and safe buildings.
Earthquake safety is drop, cover and hold; do not use lifts.
Flood response needs higher ground, clean water and avoiding contaminated water.
Relief and rehabilitation follow rescue, with attention to health and livelihoods.
example: Cyclone warnings issued days ahead allow evacuation and reduce deaths.
mistakes: Thinking disasters are only natural events.
Ignoring vulnerability and preparedness.

title: Road safety
subject: Science
summary: Road safety follows traffic rules, uses protective equipment and depends on attention and courtesy.
points: Helmets and seat belts reduce injury severity in crashes.
Pedestrians should use footpaths and crossings; drivers must yield at zebra crossings.
Speed limits, no-drink-driving and no-phone rules prevent collisions.
Vehicle maintenance, especially brakes and tyres, affects stopping distance.
First aid and calling emergency services quickly save lives.
example: Stopping distance grows with the square of speed, so doubling speed roughly quadruples braking distance.
mistakes: Thinking a short thinking time removes braking distance.
Assuming a helmet is needed only on highways.

title: Financial literacy
subject: Economics
summary: Financial literacy is the ability to manage money: budgeting, saving, borrowing wisely and understanding risk.
points: A budget compares income with planned expenditure and shows the surplus or deficit.
Savings can be held in bank deposits, post office schemes or other instruments with different risk and return.
Compound interest makes savings grow faster over long periods.
Loans must be repaid with interest; high-interest borrowing can trap households.
Insurance transfers risk, and digital payments need PIN and OTP safety.
example: ₹10,000 at 8% compound interest grows to about ₹14,693 in five years.
mistakes: Confusing simple and compound interest.
Borrowing without checking the total repayment.

title: The First World War
subject: History
summary: The First World War (1914–18) was caused by alliance rivalries, nationalism, militarism and imperial competition.
points: The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand triggered the alliance system into war.
Trench warfare on the western front caused enormous casualties.
India contributed soldiers and resources as part of the British Empire.
The Treaty of Versailles imposed reparations and territorial losses on Germany.
The war's aftermath contributed to revolution and eventually to the Second World War.
example: The Treaty of Versailles' harsh terms are often linked to later German resentment.
mistakes: Blaming the war on a single cause.
Ignoring the colonial contribution of soldiers.

title: The Second World War
subject: History
summary: The Second World War (1939–45) was fought between the Axis and Allied powers and ended with the defeat of Germany and Japan.
points: The invasion of Poland in 1939 began the war in Europe.
The Holocaust was the systematic murder of six million Jews and others by Nazi Germany.
The war was global, with major theatres in Europe, Africa and Asia-Pacific.
Atomic bombs were dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki in 1945.
The United Nations was founded in 1945 to prevent another world war.
example: The war ended in Europe in May 1945 and in Asia in September 1945.
mistakes: Saying the war began in 1941.
Treating the European and Pacific theatres as unrelated.

title: Human rights and the Universal Declaration
subject: Political Science
summary: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights, adopted in 1948, sets out rights belonging to every person.
points: Rights include life, liberty, equality, fair trial and freedom of expression.
The UDHR is not a treaty but has influenced national constitutions and laws.
Civil and political rights are paired with economic, social and cultural rights.
Human rights bodies monitor abuses but enforcement depends on states.
India's fundamental rights reflect many UDHR provisions.
example: Article 21 of the Indian Constitution on life and liberty echoes the UDHR's right to life.
mistakes: Thinking the UDHR is legally binding in itself.
Assuming rights are limited to political freedoms.
